The repository, NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer on GitHub, is the source behind the nvidia-modelopt PyPI package: a library of compression techniques covering post-training quantization, quantization-aware training, weight and attention sparsity, structured pruning, distillation, and speculative decoding. Its README states the contract plainly: you bring a Hugging Face, PyTorch, or ONNX model; ModelOpt hands back an optimized, quantized checkpoint that downstream engines like vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, and TensorRT can execute at reduced precision.

What makes the codebase worth a source tour is its architecture. Almost every technique is expressed as a mode — a self-describing object that knows how to rewrite a model, how to restore it, and how to serialize its own state. That uniformity is why a quantization call and a sparsification call look nearly identical in user code, even though one swaps nn.Linear for a fake-quantized replica and the other replaces dense attention with a masked kernel. It is also why the library can chain techniques — prune, distill, quantize, export — through one shared state manager.

This post walks the main branch as of October 2026. We map the package from its three public facades down through the quantization engine, the low-precision tensor implementations, the sparsity and pruning searchers, and the export layer that turns a quantized model into something an inference server can load. Every symbol we cite links to its actual line in the repository.

Overview: the three public namespaces (mtq, mts, mtp) sit on top of a shared mode framework; the quantization core rewrites layers and fills calibrator statistics; results flow into the Hugging Face export and the model-free ONNX path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • mtq namespace, L26 — the quantization facade imports compress, config, and conversion submodules into one flat namespace, so mtq.quantize(...) is a one-liner.
  • mtq.quantize, L310 — the central PTQ entry point that takes a model, a config dict, and a forward_loop.
  • INT8_DEFAULT_CFG, L1699 — preset configurations are loaded from YAML files shipped in the modelopt_recipes package and exposed as module constants.
  • QuantModuleRegistry, L203 — the registry that maps ordinary nn.Module types to their quantized replicas.
  • _Calibrator, L25 — the base class behind max, entropy, and MSE calibration strategies.
  • mts.sparsify, L32 — the weight-sparsity entry point driving one-shot mask searchers.
  • mtp.prune, L31 — the structured-pruning entry that searches over width and depth choices.
  • export_hf_checkpoint, L1871 — the unified Hugging Face export that writes quantized checkpoints deployable in vLLM and SGLang.
  • quantize, L122 — the model-free ONNX PTQ path, for when you have a graph rather than a training-capable model.

One Facade, Five Modes

The spine of the library is modelopt/torch/opt/mode.py. ModeDescriptor, L56 declares what a technique is called, which configuration schema it accepts, and how it should be applied; a private registry class at L277 keeps every descriptor keyed by name. Each technique module defines its own descriptor — QuantizeModeDescriptor, L84 for quantization, one for sparsity, one for distillation — and registers it with the shared machinery at import time.

The payoff is a uniform lifecycle in modelopt/torch/opt/conversion.py. ModeloptStateManager, L64 tracks which modes are currently active on a model; apply_mode, L343 is the single funnel every facade call goes through; and save, L495 serializes mode state alongside weights so a quantized checkpoint remembers how it was made. When quantization/conversion.py’s convert_to_quantized_model, L63 folds fake quantizers into real packed weights, it does so as one conversion step in this same lifecycle, not as a side door.

Five facades share this spine: mtq (quantization), mts (sparsity), mtp (pruning), modelopt.torch.distill (knowledge distillation, whose convert, L32 attaches a teacher for logit matching), and modelopt.torch.speculative (convert, L30, which bolts draft models onto a target for multi-token decoding). Distillation and speculative decoding are also how the library recovers accuracy after aggressive compression — prune a model, then teach the pruned student to behave like the original.

PTQ: Calibrate, Quantize, Convert

Post-training quantization in ModelOpt is a three-act flow. Act one: mtq.calibrate — calibrate, L73 — runs your data through the model while calibrators watch activation ranges. The calibration hierarchy starts at _Calibrator, L25; MaxCalibrator, L26 tracks a running maximum, while HistogramCalibrator, L35 builds histograms that entropy- and MSE-based clipping strategies search for better saturation points.

Act two is the rewrite. mtq.quantize walks the module tree and consults QuantModuleRegistry, L203, swapping each recognized layer class for a quantized replica that owns two children: a weight quantizer and an input quantizer, both instances of TensorQuantizer, L136. During the quantized forward pass each quantizer delegates to the autograd functions in tensor_quant.py — FakeTensorQuantFunction, L332 for integer formats, ScaledE4M3Function, L417 for FP8 — which simulate rounding without changing dtype. That simulation is what makes quantization-aware training possible: gradients flow through the fake-quant math, so a few finetuning steps can restore accuracy that pure PTQ would lose.

Act three is conversion and selection. For deployment you call the real-quantization conversion to pack weights and scales into deployable form; for hard cases there is auto_quantize, L590, which searches over per-layer format assignments under a memory or throughput budget — the mode behind it, AutoQuantizeModeDescriptor, L208, scores candidates by sensitivity, not exhaustive evaluation. A KV-cache specialist, kv_cache_auto_quant.py, searches per-layer KV formats automatically.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one line from the README:

pip install -U nvidia-modelopt[all]

The [all] extra pulls in the framework plugins (Hugging Face Transformers, diffusers, and friends) that ModelOpt discovers lazily at import. The canonical quantization snippet below is taken verbatim from the module docstring of modelopt/torch/quantization/config.py (lines 132–135), which is the same pattern every example in the repository uses:

import modelopt.torch.quantization as mtq

def forward_loop(model):
    # feed representative calibration data through the model
    for batch in calib_dataloader:
        model(**batch)

model = mtq.quantize(model, mtq.INT8_DEFAULT_CFG, forward_loop)

Three things to notice. First, quantization never touches your training code — the only new artifact is forward_loop, a plain callable that runs calibration batches. Second, the config is data: mtq.INT8_DEFAULT_CFG is a dictionary loaded from modelopt_recipes/configs/ptq/presets/model/int8.yaml, so you can deepcopy and edit it — the same docstring shows the custom-config pattern, starting from mtq.INT4_AWQ_CFG and appending an entry that disables the *lm_head* quantizer. Third, because quantization is a registered mode, mtq.quantize(model, cfg, loop) is equivalent to applying the mode through the shared state manager, so modelopt_state/save round-trips work for free. For a first experiment, a small model is enough: run the snippet on any transformers causal LM, inspect a layer (it now carries weight_quantizer and input_quantizer attributes), and call the real-quantization conversion to see packed weights.

FP8 and NVFP4: Low-Precision Paths

INT8 is the baseline, but the interesting files in this repository are the floating-point formats. Presets like FP8_DEFAULT_CFG, L1706 and NVFP4_DEFAULT_CFG, L1740 configure the same quantizer machinery for E4M3 and 4-bit floating point with two-level block scales. On the tensor side, real quantization produces packed objects deriving from BaseQuantizedTensor, L40: FP8QTensor, L33 for per-tensor FP8, and NVFP4QTensor, L67 for NVFP4, where weights are grouped into blocks of sixteen with a per-block E4M3 scale and a per-tensor FP8 scale above it. Sibling files cover MXFP8, MXFP4, INT4, and NF4 — one module per format, one dequantize contract each.

The preset YAMLs under modelopt_recipes/configs/ptq/presets/model/ are worth reading even if you never quantize: nvfp4.yaml shows exactly which module classes get weight-only versus weight-and-activation treatment, and the recipe directory also carries IQ1/IQ2-style entries for extreme weight-only compression. QAT enters through the same facade — quantized replicas are already gradient-carrying, so mts-style mode application plus an optimizer loop is all a training harness needs; NVIDIA’s QAT blog series from 2025 describes this workflow in detail for gpt-oss-class models.

One export detail deserves mention for serving: attention itself needs special handling at FP8, which is why export_onnx.py contains export_fp8_mha, L356 alongside the generic export_int8, L132 and export_fp8, L253 — fused multi-head attention has to survive graph surgery as a unit rather than being decomposed into Q/DQ pairs.

Sparsity, Pruning, and Export

The compression family beyond quantization follows the same shape. Weight sparsity exposes mts.sparsify, which drives searchers such as SparseGPTSearcher, L144 — a one-shot, Hessian-based mask search that zeroes weights and reconstructs the remaining ones to minimize output error — and MagnitudeSearcher for the simpler magnitude criterion. Attention sparsity is a different beast entirely: SparseAttentionModule, L27 replaces dense attention with token-selection logic, and the plugin in plugins/vllm.py implements ModelOptSparseAttentionBackend, L801, a drop-in flash-attention backend so a sparsified model can actually run on the vLLM server rather than merely export to it.

Pruning is search again: mtp.prune, L31 evaluates width and depth candidates, with FastNASModeDescriptor, L327 providing the channel-search mode and a binary searcher that halves or keeps blocks. The practical recipe, demonstrated in NVIDIA’s Minitron work, is prune → distill → quantize — one mode call per stage.

The export layer is where checkpoints meet serving engines. export_hf_checkpoint, L1871 writes a Hugging Face-compatible quantized checkpoint that vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM load natively; capture_quantized_weight_export_state, L375 snapshots the packed weights and scales during that process, and ExportContext, L44 dispatches per-model handlers. For deployment to classic TensorRT engines there is the ONNX path: the model-free quantizer at quantize, L122 inserts Q/DQ into an existing graph, its FP8 sibling at quantize, L140 can upgrade an INT8 graph in place via int8_to_fp8, L56, and the graph-surgery CLI at main, L64 handles the finicky edits (DQ-transpose folding, GQA replacement) that raw ONNX tooling makes painful. If your serving stack is ONNX-centric, our ONNX overview pairs well with this section.

Detail: the quantization core (config, mode, registry, fake-quant kernels) feeds both the real-quantization qtensor formats and the ONNX writers; sparsity searchers and the pruning mode converge on the same unified export that emits quantized checkpoints and TRT-LLM configs.

Honest Limits

The source is honest about what it cannot do, and so should we be. First, layout drift is real: older write-ups (including some NVIDIA docs) reference a modelopt/quantization/ package of standalone low-precision kernels, plus modelopt/core/ and modelopt/experimental/ directories — none of those exist on the current main; the low-precision tensor implementations now live under modelopt/torch/quantization/qtensor/, and preset configs moved into the separate modelopt_recipes package. Second, naming drift: mtq.int8-style preset attributes from 2024 tutorials are gone; the constants are INT8_DEFAULT_CFG and friends. Third, hardware: FP8 kernels target Hopper and newer, NVFP4 targets Blackwell; on unsupported GPUs the fake-quant simulation runs, but you are measuring accuracy potential, not speed. Fourth, accuracy is never guaranteed — INT8 SmoothQuant is usually free, W4A16 AWQ is usually close, but W4A4 NVFP4 and 2:4 sparsity are trade-offs where QAT or quantization-aware distillation is effectively mandatory. Finally, the library is pre-1.0 with a one-release deprecation window, so pin your version. Few compression toolkits make their entire surface — calibrators, fake-quant autograd, sparse attention kernels, graph surgery — this readable.
entry.summary: Walk through the ModelOpt source: INT8/FP8 PTQ and QAT flows, weight sparsity, pruning, and export paths into TensorRT and vLLM.

entry.title: TensorRT Source Tour: From ONNX Graph to Serialized CUDA Engine

link.title: TensorRT Source Tour: From ONNX Graph to Serialized CUDA Engine

entry.content:
Most deep-learning frameworks you meet day to day are executors: they take a graph, schedule its ops, and hope the kernels underneath are fast. TensorRT is a different animal. It is a compiler: it ingests a trained network, picks concrete CUDA kernels for every layer by timing candidates on your actual GPU, fuses what it can, and emits a self-contained, version-locked binary called an engine. The OSS repository we are touring today — NVIDIA/TensorRT, currently at version 11.4 — contains the public C++ API headers, the reference plugin library, the ONNX ingest layer, and the build scaffolding; the closed-source libnvinfer binary does the heavy lifting underneath them. Reading these headers is the best way to understand what the compiler promises you, which is exactly what this post walks through.

If you have followed our earlier tours of ONNX as the interchange format and of TensorRT-LLM as the LLM-focused sibling project, this is the foundation those posts stood on. TensorRT consumes ONNX as its primary input — the parser that converts a protobuf graph into TensorRT’s own INetworkDefinition lives right in this repository (well, its header does; the implementation is the onnx-tensorrt submodule). Everything else — tactic selection, plugin resolution, serialization — flows from the two dozen interfaces declared in include/.

The codebase is organized around a clean split. The build side (include/NvInfer.h) owns network construction and engine compilation; the runtime side (include/NvInferRuntime.h) owns deserialization and execution; the plugin side (include/NvInferPluginBase.h, include/NvInferRuntimeCommon.h, and the entire plugin/ tree) lets you extend the compiler with custom layers. Every public handle forwards to an opaque mImpl pointer, so the ABI can evolve without breaking recompiles — you will see the same VImpl pattern in ONNX Runtime and other ABI-sensitive projects.

TensorRT end to end: the ONNX parser fills an INetworkDefinition, the builder compiles it into a serialized engine plan, the runtime deserializes it into an ICudaEngine, and the plugin ecosystem extends the compiler with custom ops registered into a global registry.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • IParser, L191 — the ONNX front-end interface: parse(), parseFromFile(), and error reporting are the whole contract.
  • createParser, L755 — the factory that binds a parser to a network definition and a logger; from here on the parser writes layers directly into your network.
  • INetworkDefinition, L8168 — the framework-neutral graph TensorRT actually optimizes: tensors, layers, and marked outputs.
  • buildSerializedNetwork, L11739 — the compiler entry point on IBuilder: it times tactics, builds profiles, and returns a serialized engine plan as IHostMemory.
  • IRuntime, L1900 — the runtime-side factory; deserializeCudaEngine turns the plan back into a live engine.
  • deserializeCudaEngine, L2032 — where the serialized blob becomes an executable object again, plugins resolved from the registry.
  • ICudaEngine, L3143 — the immutable, per-GPU compiled artifact; it can spawn any number of execution contexts.
  • IExecutionContext, L4089 — the mutable per-stream state: set input shapes, bind device addresses, call enqueueV3.
  • IPluginRegistry, L55 — the global creator table both the builder and the runtime consult when a layer name has no built-in implementation.

The Build Side: Network, Builder, Config

Everything starts with two factory calls. createInferBuilder (NvInfer.h, L11916) gives you an IBuilder, and createNetworkV2 (NvInfer.h, L11662) mints an empty INetworkDefinition. In TensorRT 11 the explicit-batch flag that dominated 10.x documentation is gone — dynamic shapes are simply how the network works, described through optimization profiles rather than a creation flag.

Programmatically constructing a network is pleasingly mechanical: every layer type — convolutions, matmuls, elementwise ops, shuffles — is one method on INetworkDefinition, each returning a typed layer handle whose inputs and outputs are ITensor objects. You wire tensors together, then call markOutput (NvInfer.h, L8222) on whatever tensors escape the network. In practice almost nobody hand-builds graphs anymore; the ONNX parser does it, and (as the diagram shows) the parser is just another producer of the same graph IR.

The interesting object is IBuilderConfig (NvInfer.h, L10622). This is where precision flags (setFlag at NvInfer.h, L10725 for FP16, INT8, FP8, sparsity), workspace budgets via setMemoryPoolLimit (NvInfer.h, L11081), profiles, and DLA targeting all live. One builder can serve many configs; one config fully determines how aggressive the compiler gets. Memory is a first-class concern — the pool limits bound tactic workspace, persistent cache, and weight-streaming pools separately, which matters enormously once you target embedded GPUs where every megabyte is contested.

The detail view: how the ONNX ingest chain, the build/tactics surface, the runtime execution trio, and the plugin ecosystem connect — one node per source file, every node linked to the real code.

Tactics and the Timing Cache

“Tactic” is TensorRT’s word for a concrete kernel-scheduling choice for one layer: which convolution algorithm, which fusion grouping, which memory layout. At build time the compiler enumerates plausible tactics per layer and times each one on your GPU, keeping the winner. The knobs you control are TacticSource bits (NvInferRuntime.h, L2885) — in 11.x just kEDGE_MASK_CONVOLUTIONS and kJIT_CONVOLUTIONS remain, toggled through setTacticSources (NvInfer.h, L10981). The header comment on the JIT source is refreshingly honest: enabling it “may increase” engine building time.

Because re-timing hundreds of tactics on every build is painful, TensorRT persists the measurements. createTimingCache (NvInfer.h, L11016) returns an ITimingCache (NvInfer.h, L10209) that you attach to the config; after a build, ITimingCache::serialize (NvInfer.h, L10223) hands you a blob you can check in next to your model. CI farms love this: build once per driver/GPU family, replay the cache everywhere. The catch is documented right in the header — a cache “must be generated by a build of exact same version,” so caches, like engines, are version-locked artifacts rather than durable data.

The end product of all this measurement is not a live object but bytes: buildSerializedNetwork (NvInfer.h, L11739) returns IHostMemory containing the plan. Engines are only consumable by the same TensorRT version on the same compute capability — a deliberate trade: the compiler freezes GPU-specific decisions in exchange for not shipping a kernel-selection runtime. Serialization is also how the ecosystem moves engines around; serving stacks like Triton Inference Server treat the plan file as the deployable unit, exactly the role an .onnx file plays for ONNX Runtime.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s fast path is one command: pip install tensorrt — the Python package wraps the same C++ API, so the concepts below transfer one-to-one. For the full OSS build you need CUDA 12.9 or 13.4, CMake ≥ 3.31, then git clone -b main https://github.com/nvidia/TensorRT TensorRT && git submodule update --init --recursive, and the release tarballs from NVIDIA provide libnvinfer plus the trtexec CLI you can use to sanity-check engines without writing code.

Here is the whole build-to-execute flow in C++, using only interfaces we verified in the tree above:

#include "NvInfer.h"
#include "NvOnnxParser.h"

using namespace nvinfer1;

Logger logger;  // your ILogger implementation

// Build side: compile model.onnx into a serialized engine plan.
auto builder = std::unique_ptr<IBuilder>(createInferBuilder(logger));
auto network = std::unique_ptr<INetworkDefinition>(builder->createNetworkV2(0));
auto parser  = std::unique_ptr<IParser>(nvonnxparser::createParser(*network, logger));
parser->parseFromFile("model.onnx", static_cast<int>(ILogger::Severity::kWARNING));

auto config = std::unique_ptr<IBuilderConfig>(builder->createBuilderConfig());
auto plan   = std::unique_ptr<IHostMemory>(
    builder->buildSerializedNetwork(*network, *config));

// Runtime side: deserialize and execute on a CUDA stream.
auto runtime = std::unique_ptr<IRuntime>(createInferRuntime(logger));
auto engine  = std::unique_ptr<ICudaEngine>(
    runtime->deserializeCudaEngine(plan->data(), plan->size()));
auto context = std::unique_ptr<IExecutionContext>(engine->createExecutionContext());
// set tensor addresses, then: context->enqueueV3(stream);

Every symbol in that snippet is real: createInferBuilder (NvInfer.h, L11916), createNetworkV2 (NvInfer.h, L11662), createBuilderConfig (NvInfer.h, L11635), parseFromFile (NvOnnxParser.h, L222), and on the runtime side createInferRuntime (NvInferRuntime.h, L5226), deserializeCudaEngine (NvInferRuntime.h, L2032), and createExecutionContext (NvInferRuntime.h, L3301). Actual GPU work is submitted asynchronously by enqueueV3 (NvInferRuntime.h, L4791) on a stream you own — there is no blocking execute dance anymore, and multi-stream serving is just more contexts on more streams.

The Plugin Registry and IPluginV3

When the parser meets an ONNX op TensorRT does not implement, or when you have a hand-written CUDA kernel no graph rewrite can express, plugins are the escape hatch. The current contract is IPluginV3 (NvInferPluginBase.h, L205), a versioned interface whose key move is the capability split: a plugin object returns separate interfaces for the kCORE, kBUILD, and kRUNTIME phases. Build-phase code answers “what output shapes and formats can you support”; runtime-phase code does the actual launch. The cleanest example in the tree is ROIAlignV3 (roiAlignPlugin.h, L58), which inherits IPluginV3, IPluginV3OneCore, IPluginV3OneBuild, and IPluginV3OneRuntime on one class.

Registration is a two-lane system. Lane one: REGISTER_TENSORRT_PLUGIN(Creator) (NvInferRuntime.h, L5271) is a static-initializer macro that self-registers a creator when the plugin library loads — see it live at skipLayerNormPlugin.cpp, L41 for the fused Skip-LayerNorm V3 plugin (skipLayerNormPlugin.h, L46). Lane two: the monolithic bundled library calls initLibNvInferPlugins (inferPlugin.cpp, L171), which pushes dozens of creators — ROIAlign, EfficientNMS, InstanceNormalization, GroupNorm — into the PluginCreatorRegistry (inferPlugin.cpp, L152) through registerCreator (NvInferRuntimeCommon.h, L158). Both lanes end in the same registry the builder consults mid-compile.

The tree also documents history. GroupNormalizationPlugin (groupNormalizationPlugin.h, L37) still implements the older IPluginV2DynamicExt shape, with the familiar configurePlugin / enqueue rhythm and the actual CUDA launch at groupNormalizationPlugin.cpp, L127. If you write a new plugin today, target V3 — the V2 surface is kept for compatibility and is not recommended for new work. Note that most of these plugin kernels are plain CUDA in this repo (dive into plugin/common/kernels/ for the shared math); they are an underrated tutorial on writing production tensor kernels, complementary to the template-library style of CUTLASS.

Runtime: Engines, Contexts, and Streams

The runtime side is deliberately tiny. createInferRuntime hands you an IRuntime; its one big method is deserializeCudaEngine. An ICudaEngine is immutable — you can even re-serialize it with serialize (NvInferRuntime.h, L3201) or query which tactic sources actually made it into the compiled plan via getTacticSources (NvInferRuntime.h, L3651). All mutable state lives in IExecutionContext: input shape binding, address binding, and stream-ordered launch. One engine, many contexts, is the canonical serving pattern — each worker thread gets its own context over the shared weights.

Two runtime details deserve a nod. First, hardware targeting: IRuntime::setDLACore (NvInferRuntime.h, L1919) and the builder’s getNbDLACores (NvInfer.h, L11603) expose NVIDIA’s on-SoC deep-learning accelerator as just another backend the same engine format covers. Second, plugin lifetimes at runtime: the deserializer resolves plugin creators through getPluginRegistry (NvInferRuntime.h, L5207), so any engine containing custom ops needs those plugins loaded before deserialization — a classic deployment footgun that the registry design makes visible rather than silent.

Honest Limits

The trade-offs are real and worth naming before you adopt TensorRT for a project:

  • The open source is not the whole compiler. This repository ships headers, the plugin library, and the parser. The tactic-search heuristics, the fusers, and the kernel library itself live in the closed libnvinfer binary. You can read the contract but not the optimizer — the inverse of projects like OpenVINO or ONNX Runtime, where the graph transformations are all in-tree.
  • Build latency is the price of throughput. Tactic timing plus JIT convolution sources can turn an engine build into minutes-long, GPU-pegged work. Timing caches help, but a cache is only valid for the exact TensorRT version (the header says so verbatim), and every version upgrade re-opens the search.
  • Engines are version-locked and hardware-specific. A plan built on one GPU generation will not deserialize on another, and forward compatibility across TensorRT releases is not a design goal. That makes engine artifacts closer to compiled binaries than to portable models — plan your artifact storage accordingly.
  • NVIDIA-only, full stop. No AMD, no Apple, no CPU fallback path. If your deployment matrix is heterogeneous, you will maintain a second serving chain for non-CUDA targets.
  • ONNX coverage has holes. Unsupported ops throw you into plugin territory, which means writing and maintaining CUDA for exactly the layers that made you reach for TensorRT in the first place.

None of these caveats change the punchline: for fixed models on NVIDIA GPUs, the compiler’s willingness to measure before committing is why TensorRT-compiled engines routinely beat interpreted execution by healthy margins. The source tour above should give you the map to go from “it’s fast” to knowing precisely which interface is responsible for the speed — and where to look when something is not.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of NVIDIA/TensorRT: INetworkDefinition, IBuilder tactics and timing caches, the ONNX parser flow, the plugin registry, and engine serialization.

entry.title: TFLite Micro: How Neural Network Inference Fits in 256 KB Without malloc

link.title: TFLite Micro: How Neural Network Inference Fits in 256 KB Without malloc

entry.content:
Every inference runtime we have toured in this series — TensorFlow, ONNX Runtime, llama.cpp — assumes a fat host: gigabytes of RAM, an allocator that can hand out memory at will, maybe a GPU on the side. The repo under the microscope this time lives in a different world entirely. tflite-micro is the TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM) runtime, and it is designed to run a neural network on a Cortex-M0 with 256 KB of RAM, a DSP with no operating system, or an ESP32 burning a few milliamps. There is no heap, no malloc, sometimes not even a filesystem — and yet the same .tflite flatbuffer that a desktop TensorFlow deployment would consume runs, byte for byte, on a microcontroller.

The trick is that TFLM does not load a model in any dynamic sense. It never copies tensor data, never parses the flatbuffer into heap objects, and never allocates anything after a one-time setup call. Instead, you hand it a single statically allocated byte array — the tensor arena — and it carves everything it needs out of that arena with pure pointer arithmetic. If you have read our NCNN tour, which does aggressive mobile inference but still runs on a real OS with a heap, the contrast is instructive: TFLM removes the allocator from the equation entirely, because on bare metal there is nobody to ask for more memory.

This post walks the actual source: how the flatbuffer is mapped zero-copy, how the MicroAllocator and its memory planners overlay activation buffers inside the arena, how MicroInterpreter drives a two-phase execution flow, and how the kernel layer splits into a portable reference and per-MCU optimized backends like CMSIS-NN. Two diagrams generated from the repository structure anchor the tour.

TFLite Micro at a glance: a zero-copy flatbuffer model, one static arena split by the MicroAllocator and a memory planner, and an operator layer resolved through a user-sized op resolver down to portable or CMSIS-NN kernels.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • tflite::GetModel, L25818 — casts your raw .tflite bytes onto generated flatbuffer accessors. No copy, no parsing, no allocation; validation happens lazily as fields are read.
  • MicroInterpreter, L45 — the user-facing facade. Its constructor takes a Model*, an op resolver, and your raw arena pointer; the primary overload, L55 is the whole dependency list of the runtime.
  • AllocateTensors, L189 — the one-time setup phase: builds subgraph allocations, runs every kernel’s Init and Prepare, then commits the static memory plan.
  • MicroAllocator, L128 — the class that turns one uint8_t buffer into persistent structs, activation tensors, and scratch space, with the factory, L136 selecting the planner.
  • SingleArenaBufferAllocator, L32 — the bump allocator underneath, growing a persistent tail up and a temporary head down inside the same arena.
  • GreedyMemoryPlanner, L47 — the default planner that overlays activation buffers whose lifetimes never intersect.
  • MicroMutableOpResolver, L49 — a compile-time-sized array holding only the operators your model actually uses.
  • InvokeSubgraph, L245 — the execution hot loop: for each operator, call its registration’s invoke, then reset the temp region.
  • MicroInterpreterContext, L34 — the MicroContext facade through which kernels request tensors, scratch buffers, and profiling.

Loading a Model Without malloc

The foundation of everything is the flatbuffer format itself, shared with the parent TensorFlow Lite runtime. Flatbuffers serialize structures so that the serialized bytes are the in-memory representation: fields are accessed through vtable-relative offsets, so GetModel(buf) is literally a pointer cast plus a version check. There is a subtlety worth appreciating: the model is typically placed in flash (on embedded targets, often baked into the firmware image as a C array), and TFLM reads it directly from flash without ever touching RAM. The weights you trained on a workstation become const uint8_t bytes in the .text section of your firmware.

Everything mutable lives elsewhere. The TfLiteEvalTensor, L308 struct is the stripped-down, RAM-friendly cousin of the desktop TfLiteTensor: just data pointer, shape, and type, sized for the array-of-structs layout the allocator builds. Quantized models matter enormously here — an int8 tensor occupies a quarter of the flash and RAM that a float32 one does, and the hello world example, L139 demonstrates the dequantization dance ((int8_value - zero_point) * scale) at the output boundary.

The model-side metadata that kernels need — stride, dilation, activation function — is parsed out of the flatbuffer exactly once, during setup. The parser functions live in flatbuffer_conversions.cc; for instance ParseConv2D, L484 decodes Conv2DOptions into a Conv2DParams struct allocated from the arena’s persistent tail. This is one of the few places TFLM does transform flatbuffer data into native structs, and even that transformation allocates no heap memory — the BuiltinDataAllocator it receives hands out arena memory.

MicroInterpreter: AllocateTensors Then Invoke

The public API has exactly two phases, and the hello world test is a faithful minimal client. Its main(), L151 calls InitializeTarget, L24 for board bring-up, builds a resolver, and constructs an interpreter over a 3 KB stack array. Then AllocateTensors() and Invoke() — everything else is tensor I/O.

AllocateTensors is where the interesting orchestration happens. Reading its implementation, L189 top to bottom: StartModelAllocation walks the flatbuffer and allocates the persistent bookkeeping (node/registration arrays, eval tensor arrays), then PrepareNodeAndRegistrationDataFromFlatbuffer, L96 resolves each operator through the resolver and stores its TFLMRegistration*. Next the context switches into kInit and then kPrepare states, and every kernel gets its Init and Prepare callbacks — this is when a conv kernel picks tiling parameters, quantization multipliers, and requests scratch buffers. Only after all kernels have spoken does FinishModelAllocation, L195 compute the final activation layout, because only now are all buffer sizes and lifetimes known.

After allocation, Invoke, L271 is almost boring, and that is the point: it delegates to InvokeSubgraph, L245, which is a for-loop over operators calling registration->invoke(context_, node), L276. One line right after deserves attention: ResetTempAllocations, L285. Kernels allocate their TfLiteTensor views from the arena’s temporary head section; between ops that section is rewound to zero, so a graph of a thousand operators costs no more temp memory than a graph of one. Kernels that need to read tensors call back through the context — GetEvalTensor, L98 returns the zero-copy view by index.

The Tensor Arena and Its Planners

The tensor arena is the entire memory contract: a uint8_t array whose size you must guess up front. Internally it is managed as two regions growing toward each other — the persistent tail holds structs and op data that live as long as the interpreter, the head holds temporaries and the activation plan. The split is implemented by SingleArenaBufferAllocator, L32, which delegates to a PersistentArenaBufferAllocator, L31 for the tail and a NonPersistentArenaBufferAllocator, L30 for the head. If the two pointers cross, allocation fails with an error — there is no garbage collection and no second chance.

The activation buffers themselves are placed by a memory planner, an idea borrowed from compiler register allocation. The interface at MicroMemoryPlanner, L46 is tiny: add buffers with their usage intervals, get back offsets. The default GreedyMemoryPlanner, L47 sorts buffers by size and, via AddBuffer, L109, drops each one into the smallest gap where it does not overlap in time with already-placed buffers — classic interval scheduling, and remarkably effective since CNN activations tend to die young. The lifetime data comes from AllocationInfoBuilder::CreateAllocationInfo, L104, which marks each tensor’s first and last use by scanning the subgraph’s operator order. The final layout is committed in CommitStaticMemoryPlan, L1116, which writes the chosen offsets into every eval tensor.

A LinearMemoryPlanner, L27 exists as the conservative alternative: buffers are laid out strictly in execution order, which wastes more memory but behaves predictably and supports the preserve_all_tensors debugging feature. Because the whole plan is computed offline relative to a fixed arena, the planner runs inside the arena too — the greedy planner even takes its own scratch buffer as a constructor argument, practicing what it preaches.

Op Resolution and the Kernel Contract

The kernel contract is a single C struct. TFLMRegistration, L325 carries four function pointers (init, prepare, invoke, free) plus a builtin code or custom name, and the entire kernel ecosystem plugs into the interpreter through it. Where the desktop TensorFlow runtime registers hundreds of ops at startup, TFLM inverts the model: you tell the resolver what to include. MicroMutableOpResolver, L49 is templated on a compile-time count tOpCount, and each Add* call — AddConv2D, L207, AddFullyConnected, custom ops through AddCustom, L93 — copies a registration plus its flatbuffer parser into that array. Resolution during prepare is a linear scan in FindOp, L55; for five to ten ops that is faster than any hash table.

The kernels themselves come in two flavors sharing one contract. The portable reference implementations are plain readable C++ — ConvEval, L30 type-dispatches down to the reference math in Conv, L28, which is the textbook loop nest. For real deployments on Arm cores, the build-time OPTIMIZED_KERNEL_DIR=cmsis_nn flag swaps the innards for CMSIS-NN: the registration in cmsis_nn/conv.cc, L487 exposes the same Register_CONV_2D, but EvalInt8, L346 calls Arm’s DSP-optimized kernels underneath. This same directory pattern covers Xtensa (HiFi cores), Ethos-U NPU dispatch, and others — and it is the microcontroller sibling of what XNNPACK does for server and mobile CPU inference (our XNNPACK tour covers the same dispatch idea at larger scale). A decent part of the kernel directory exists purely to be swapped: Register_DEPTHWISE_CONV_2D, L184, Register_FULLY_CONNECTED, L359, and Register_SOFTMAX, L86 all follow the identical prepare-eval-register shape.

The framework comparison is worth spelling out. Compared to graph-compiler stacks like TVM, which generate fused C code per model, TFLM ships a pre-compiled interpreter and asks the model to conform; compared to end-to-end device runtimes like ExecuTorch, it is radically smaller and dumber — deliberately. The .tflite format itself is the same one ONNX users reach for via converters in spirit, though the details differ; the common thread across all of these is that the runtime cost scales with ops you select, not ops that exist.

From Install to Your First Model

There is no pip wheel for your dev board; TFLM is a source-first project meant to be vendored or compiled into your firmware. Clone the repo and you can build the canonical hello world example — a two-layer fully connected network approximating a sine wave — directly on your host machine first. The README-verified Make flow builds every dependency and compiles the test with the host toolchain:

make -f tensorflow/lite/micro/tools/make/Makefile test_hello_world_test

The equivalent under Bazel (also from the checked-out docs) is:

bazel run tensorflow/lite/micro/examples/hello_world:hello_world_test

Passing prints ~~~ALL TESTS PASSED~~~. The test source doubles as the shortest possible client. Stripped to its skeleton, the exact pattern verified against the checked-out tree is:

#include "tensorflow/lite/micro/micro_interpreter.h"
#include "tensorflow/lite/micro/micro_mutable_op_resolver.h"
#include "tensorflow/lite/micro/examples/hello_world/models/hello_world_float_model_data.h"

namespace {
using OpResolver = tflite::MicroMutableOpResolver<1>;
TfLiteStatus RegisterOps(OpResolver& resolver) {
  return resolver.AddFullyConnected();  // the only op this model uses
}
}  // namespace

TfLiteStatus RunInference() {
  const tflite::Model* model =
      ::tflite::GetModel(g_hello_world_float_model_data);
  OpResolver op_resolver;
  TF_LITE_ENSURE_STATUS(RegisterOps(op_resolver));

  constexpr int kTensorArenaSize = 3000;
  alignas(16) uint8_t tensor_arena[kTensorArenaSize];

  tflite::MicroInterpreter interpreter(model, op_resolver, tensor_arena,
                                       kTensorArenaSize);
  TF_LITE_ENSURE_STATUS(interpreter.AllocateTensors());

  interpreter.input(0)->data.f[0] = 1.f;
  TF_LITE_ENSURE_STATUS(interpreter.Invoke());
  float y = interpreter.output(0)->data.f[0];
  return kTfLiteOk;
}

Three practical notes before you port this to a board. First, arena sizing: the example’s 3000 bytes is a guess, and the right tool for a real guess is the recording variant — run under RecordingMicroInterpreter, L37 and its allocator prints per-section usage, including arena_used_bytes() after AllocateTensors. Second, run it under MicroProfiler, L29 to get cycle counts per operator as CSV before you optimize anything. Third, the same Makefile cross-compiles: pass TARGET=cortex_m_generic OPTIMIZED_KERNEL_DIR=cmsis_nn and the tree produces binaries for Arm boards — the toolchain layer is exactly where per-MCU quirks surface.

Honest Limits

The static-memory design is the whole point, and it imposes real constraints. The arena is sized for the worst case at setup time and never renegotiated; if your arena is too small, AllocateTensors fails outright, and if it is too large you have permanently wasted RAM. There is no dynamic allocation at run time at all — models with data-dependent shapes, dynamic control flow beyond the explicit IF/WHILE operator support, or anything requiring new tensors mid-inference does not fit the framework. Even MicroMutableOpResolver capacity is a template constant: exceed your declared tOpCount and registration fails at build time (by design).

Op coverage is a second honest gap. TFLM supports a curated subset of the TensorFlow Lite op set, and the supported subset is int8-quantization-first; float16, complex control flow, and exotic layers frequently require either model surgery, custom op registration, or simply do not work. Kernel performance is uneven across targets: the portable reference is fine for correctness work but can be an order of magnitude off optimized paths, and the optimized backends have per-target toolchain demands — CMSIS-NN needs Arm GCC/Clang with specific flags, Xtensa needs the vendor’s toolchain and NNLib, Ethos-U needs the driver stack. The Windows and x86 paths work for CI but nobody ships a product on them.

Finally, debugging is spartan. Error strings are stripped in production builds (TF_LITE_STRIP_ERROR_STRINGS) to save flash, so failures often surface as a bare status code; the layer-by-layer debugging tools and the recording allocator help, but expect to reason about arena layout by hand. None of this is a flaw so much as the honest price of running inference where every byte has a name and no allocator exists to ask for more.
entry.summary: A source tour of TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers: zero-copy flatbuffer loading, the MicroInterpreter, static memory planning over a tensor arena, and portable versus CMSIS-NN optimized kernels.

entry.title: PyTorch/XLA: Inside the Bridge from Eager PyTorch to TPU Hardware

link.title: PyTorch/XLA: Inside the Bridge from Eager PyTorch to TPU Hardware

entry.content:
Most deep learning engineers meet PyTorch as an eager framework: every op fires a kernel the moment you call it. On a TPU, that model of execution does not work. TPUs are fed by a compiler — XLA, the Accelerated Linear Algebra compiler that also powers JAX and TensorFlow — and a compiler needs to see a whole computation before it can schedule buffers, fuse ops, and tile matrix multiplies across a systolic array. PyTorch/XLA (the torch_xla package, developed in the pytorch/xla repository) is the machinery that makes an eager framework speak fluent compiler.

The deal it offers is simple to state and subtle to implement. You keep writing ordinary PyTorch code — modules, autograd, optimizers, data loaders — but tensors live on a special device called xla, and nothing executes when you call an op. Instead, every op appends a node to a lazily-traced graph. When you call xm.mark_step(), the accumulated graph is lowered to XLA HLO, compiled, cached against a hash, and pushed to the device for execution. This is the same architectural bargain JAX makes explicitly with jit, but grafted onto PyTorch’s eager semantics so that existing code mostly runs unchanged.

This post is a source tour of how that bargain is honored, based on a fresh checkout of pytorch/xla. We will walk the full stack: the xm Python API, the C++ lazy-tensor core that traces and lowers graphs, the PJRT runtime that owns device buffers, the SPMD sharding layer for multi-chip training, and the newer Dynamo bridge that lets torch.compile target XLA directly.

The PyTorch/XLA stack: Python entry points on the left, the C++ lowering core in the middle, the PJRT runtime underneath, and the SPMD sharding layer wrapping it all for multi-device runs.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • xm.xla_device, L122 is the front door: it hands you a torch.device('xla') that any PyTorch model can be moved to.
  • xm.mark_step, L1031 is the synchronization beat of the whole system — the point where traced graphs get compiled and shipped.
  • set_device_type, L41 in the xr runtime module selects the PJRT device type (CPU, TPU, GPU plugin) and queries world size and ordinals.
  • extract_compiled_graph, L670 is the Dynamo bridge that converts a captured FX graph into XLA IR instead of tracing op-by-op.
  • SyncTensorsGraphInternal, L1533 is the C++ heart: it hashes the traced graph, hits the compilation cache, or compiles fresh HLO.
  • LoweringContext::GetOutputOp, L255 turns lazy IR nodes into concrete XLA ops during lowering.
  • PjRtComputationClient::Compile, L544 hands the HLO module to the PJRT client, which executes it against real device buffers.
  • mark_sharding, L685 annotates a tensor with an OpSharding spec so the SPMD partitioner can split one program across a mesh of chips.

Lazy Tensors: Pay Only When You Sync

The first thing to internalize is that an xla tensor is not a pointer to device memory the way a CUDA tensor is. In the C++ core, an XLATensor holds either device data, an IR node describing a pending computation, or a view — and the three states migrate lazily. When you compute loss = model(x).sum(), nothing executes. When you call loss.backward() and then xm.optimizer_step(...), the framework accumulates the forward graph, the backward graph, and the gradient update into one big computation, then lowers all of it at the next mark_step.

This design has a beautiful consequence: the unit of compilation is whatever happens between two mark_step calls, and PyTorch/XLA compiles that whole region at once, fusing elementwise chains and materializing only what it must. It also has an obvious cost, which we will return to in the limits section: tracing happens on the host, in C++, one op at a time.

The xm module is the Python-facing contract. Beyond xla_device and mark_step, it carries the collectives that predate the SPMD layer: xm.all_reduce, L396 reduces gradients across replicas with a configurable REDUCE_SUM/REDUCE_MEAN type, and xm.optimizer_step, L1169 bundles gradient all-reduce, the optimizer step, and an optional barrier into one call. The top-level torch_xla package wraps these in a cleaner surface — torch_xla.sync, L78 is the modern spelling of mark_step.

Inside the C++ Lowering Layer

Everything below the Python API happens in torch_xla/csrc. The flow from Python call to device execution is a chain of four stages, each visible in the source.

Stage one is dispatch. InitXlaBackend, L254 registers XLA as a backend with PyTorch’s dispatcher, so calling an op on an xla tensor routes into torch_xla’s implementations rather than ATen kernels. Stage two is tracing: each op implementation in tensor_methods.cpp appends a node to the lazy IR graph — for collectives, tensor_methods.cpp all_reduce, L750 constructs an AllReduce node carrying the reduction type and replica groups, and the node kinds themselves are declared in ops/xla_ops.cpp, L5 as OpKindWrapper constants like xla::cross_replica_sum.

Stage three is the graph executor. When a sync fires, XLAGraphExecutor collects the live tensors for the device, walks the IR in post-order through a LoweringContext, and produces an HLO computation. Crucially, the executor hashes the graph — parameters, IR structure, even auto-sharding configuration — and consults a cache of compiled computations before compiling anything. A cache hit skips straight to execution; this is why steady-state training on XLA is fast even though step one pays a large compile bill. The hash-then-compile-then-schedule sequence lives in TryRunCachedSync, L1245 and the Compile routine it guards.

Stage four is the runtime boundary. The lowering output is an HLO module; the device wants buffers and an executable. The singleton client returned by GetComputationClient, L53 is a PjRtComputationClient (or, experimentally, an IFRT client), and its Compile and TransferToDevice methods are the seam where PyTorch data structures become PJRT buffers. PJRT is the same device API JAX uses, which is what makes cross-framework tooling on TPUs possible at all.

From Install to Your First Model

The README’s stable-build instructions for a TPU VM are refreshingly short:

pip install torch==2.8.0 'torch_xla[tpu]==2.8.0'

The tpu extra pulls in libtpu, the PJRT plugin that talks to the chip. On CPU-only machines (or GPUs via plugins), the package installs from source or from project-specific indexes; there is a full matrix of wheels in the repository README. Once installed, a minimal end-to-end training step uses only APIs you can find in the tree:

import torch
import torch_xla.core.xla_model as xm

device = xm.xla_device()
model = torch.nn.Linear(128, 64).to(device)
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

x = torch.randn(16, 128, device=device)
loss = model(x).sum()      # traced, not executed
loss.backward()            # backward graph traced too
xm.optimizer_step(opt)     # all-reduce grads + step
xm.mark_step()             # <- compile & execute happens HERE

The mental model to keep: the loop body is trace-compile-cache-execute. On the first step you pay the compiler; on later steps, the graph hash matches and the cached executable runs. xm.optimizer_step is doing double duty — it wraps reduce_gradients plus optimizer.step() — which is why real examples like test/test_train_mp_mnist.py in the repository call exactly this sequence.

Scaling Out: PJRT Processes and SPMD Meshes

Multi-device execution changed shape a few years ago when torch_xla moved from XRT (an RPC server model) to PJRT. In the PJRT world, replication is process-based: one process per device (or one process hosting several devices), and the Python-level launcher for that is pjrt.spawn, L186, which xmp.spawn in xla_multiprocessing.py, L10 forwards to. Each process binds to its device, and collectives like xm.all_reduce coordinate across processes through the runtime rather than through a central server. Data feeding uses MpDeviceLoader (parallel_loader.py, L253), which shards batches per device and issues the step-closure sync at the right moment. If you have used Accelerate or DeepSpeed, the mental model of “launcher plus wrapped loader plus gradient sync” will feel familiar.

The newer story is SPMD: instead of N processes each running a full program copy, you run one program across a mesh of devices and let the XLA compiler partition it. You opt in with xr.use_spmd(), build a mesh, and annotate tensors. The Mesh class (xla_sharding.py, L38) takes device IDs, a mesh shape, and axis names; get_1d_mesh covers the simple data-parallel case; and mark_sharding attaches an OpSharding to a tensor. The DTensor-flavored entry points are xla_distribute_tensor and xla_distribute_module in spmd/api.py, L110, which accept PyTorch DeviceMesh objects and partition specs — deliberately mirroring the upstream torch.distributed.tensor API. Under the hood the annotations flow into xla_sharding_util.cpp, which propagates sharding through the IR so the HLO SPMD partitioner can slice the computation.

The Dynamo Bridge: torch.compile on XLA

Lazy tracing was built one op at a time, in C++, and it shows in CPU profiles for big models. The modern alternative is to let PyTorch’s own compiler capture the program. torch_xla.compile (torch_xla.py, L114) uses the Dynamo bridge in _dynamo/dynamo_bridge.py: Dynamo produces an FX graph, the bridge runs extract_compiled_graph to convert FX nodes into XLA IR — including an analysis pass that partitions nodes into XLA-executable and CPU-fallback regions — and returns a callable that executes the lowered computation. Because Dynamo’s symbolic reasoning handles dynamic shapes and guards more gracefully than op-by-op tracing, this path is where most new investment is going.

There is also an experimental second backend, dynamo_backend2.py, which routes FX graphs through torchax and JAX’s compiler tooling instead of the native C++ tracer — evidence that the long-term direction is converging on the shared OpenXLA stack that also serves IREE and the rest of the XLA ecosystem, much as TensorFlow standardized on XLA years ago.

Honest Limits

Lazy tensors are a tax as well as a gift. Tracing runs op-by-op on the host, and for large models the host can become the bottleneck — the repository’s own performance docs discuss “tracing-bound” workloads where TPUs sit idle waiting for the CPU, and why the C++11-ABI wheels measurably improve flops utilization on exactly those workloads.

Recompilation is the second recurring cost. The cache is keyed by graph hash, so dynamic shapes (variable sequence lengths, data-dependent control flow) produce fresh hashes and fresh compiles. Code that reshapes itself every step can spend all its time in the compiler; the standard mitigations are padding, bucketing, Dynamo’s shape handling, or explicit graph breaks.

Hardware access is the third practical constraint. TPU code requires a TPU VM (or the CPU/GPU PJRT plugins, which are functional but not the main audience), the wheels are Linux-only — Windows users need WSL — and libtpu is distributed for specific Python versions, so version pinning between Python, torch, and torch_xla matters. Finally, some things you take for granted on CUDA tensors (certain in-place mutations and views) fall back to CPU; the metrics module (torch_xla.debug.metrics) will tell you when a fallback fired, and it is worth checking after your first run.

None of these limits are fatal — Google trains Gemini-scale models through this stack — but they shape a different engineering rhythm than eager GPU work: you profile compilation counts and graph hashes, not just kernel times.

Where PyTorch/XLA Fits

In the widening zoo of execution backends, torch_xla occupies a specific niche: it is the sanctioned path from eager PyTorch semantics onto XLA-compatible accelerators, sharing compiler infrastructure with JAX while keeping your training loop recognizably PyTorch. If your deployment target is a TPU pod, it is not optional; if your target is a laptop or a phone, alternatives like Executorch fit better. But understanding how a lazily-traced graph becomes an HLO program that a compiler partitions across a mesh is one of the most transferable mental models in modern ML infrastructure — and the pytorch/xla source tree, unusually for this kind of project, lets you read every layer of it in one afternoon.
